title: You Don't Have to Pass Childhood Adversity On: Telling Your Own Story Breaks the Cycle
dek: The London Parent-Child Project found that whether parents can tell their childhood in a coherent, flexible way predicts secure attachment better than the childhood itself — reflective functioning is a trainable skill.
why: Medium information density, but the idea that intergenerational transmission can be interrupted by narrative has directly usable judgment value for founders who care about parenting.
who: Founders and managers who have children or plan to, especially those worried their own childhood will shape how they parent and looking for something actionable to hold onto.
skip: The first roughly two minutes of anniversary celebration and five-star review requests can be skipped.

points.h: The key to secure attachment is reunion, not separation
points.body: In the Strange Situation, the child is briefly left in an unfamiliar room, and the crying at separation matters far less than the reaction at reunion: whether the child actively approaches, seeks contact, and can go back to playing once "refuelled." Steele says securely attached children have a strategy — they know what to do when they feel bad. Insecure attachment also comes with strategies, just worse ones: avoidant children look calm, but their cortisol keeps rising; ambivalent children are picked up and then want down, unable to return to exploration.

points.h: Avoidant and ambivalent are both the child's best solution
points.body: Steele stresses that avoidant is not coldness — it is a child learning by nine to twelve months that "no one will come when I feel bad," so they push the pain away and go play with toys; ambivalent children amplify their emotions to win closeness. Both are organized strategies, the best defence available under the circumstances. Sarah adds: it doesn't work, but it's the best thing the child can come up with. That explains why blaming a child for being "too clingy" or "not clingy enough" is wrong — it was adapted.

Mary Main used fright without solution to describe disorganized attachment: the child desperately needs this attachment figure to protect them and is also afraid of this person, and with two irreconcilable facts holding at once, behaviour breaks down — when the parent returns the child moves away, freezes, huddles in a corner. Steele warns the term has been overused by the public, drifting from its originally strict observational definition. It is not a strategy the child chose; it is the system shutting down.

points.h: Even in secure attachment, attuned moments are under half
points.body: Steele gives a counterintuitive number: even for securely attached mothers and children, genuinely "attuned" moments are under 50%. The child learns precisely from the mismatches — mum didn't catch it, so the child finds a way to pull her back. In Tronick's still face experiment, the infant reaches out, smiles, calls out to bring mum back. But with too many mismatches, the child gives up and turns to the defensive modes of avoidance or ambivalence. So perfection is not the goal; repair is.

points.h: Cosleeping until seven won't buy you secure attachment
points.body: Steele names the "recipe-style" practices in attachment parenting directly — cosleeping until five or seven, for instance — saying they have no one-to-one correspondence with secure attachment, and no such requirement exists in the original literature. What secure attachment actually is: following the child's lead, making the child feel they are in your mind, and responding promptly especially when they are upset. She also criticises "pre-emptive gratification": rushing to feed a child before they have noticed they are hungry erases the child's agency to recognise their own state and find their own way.

points.h: A child's attachment type can be predicted before birth
points.body: The London Parent-Child Project ran the Adult Attachment Interview with 100 couples in late pregnancy, then the Strange Situation with the mother at 12 months and with the father at 18 months. Result: from how parents talked about their own childhood before the baby was born alone, the child's attachment type could be predicted at 12 months (for mothers) and 18 months (for fathers). Steele showed the results to Bowlby, and Bowlby said they couldn't even predict the weather, yet here they were predicting something so subtle.

points.h: What breaks the cycle isn't being unharmed, it's being able to tell it clearly
points.body: The study grouped the sample by childhood adversity (parent hospitalisation, unemployment over three months, low socioeconomic status, and so on). The key finding: parents who had experienced adversity but could narrate their childhood in a way that references mental states — understanding what was going on in their parents' heads back then — had a significantly higher rate of securely attached children; among parents who had experienced adversity without that capacity, the vast majority of children were insecurely attached. Steele sums up secure attachment in two words, flexibility and coherence: does your story have a beginning, a middle and an end, and does it hold up to questioning.

points.h: To be the one who breaks the cycle, first learn to observe yourself
points.body: Steele's concrete advice: get familiar with the basic concepts of attachment, learn to observe yourself, and especially watch your own triggers — work out what makes you so sad and angry at this moment that should be beautiful. She does not think yelling at a child is a good approach, but short of cases that constitute abuse, stepping away for thirty seconds and saying "Mummy is very angry right now, I need a moment" is itself modelling for the child that emotions have strategies for being handled. She also suggests finding a clinician to see your own patterns with, because people are pattern-generating creatures, and the attachment system is at heart emotion regulation.

terms.def: A roughly 20-minute laboratory procedure designed by Mary Ainsworth that observes infant attachment types through brief separation and reunion.
An interview developed by Mary Main that assesses parents' attachment representations through the way they narrate their childhood experiences.
The capacity to understand the mental states (thoughts, feelings, intentions) behind one's own and others' behaviour; it is trainable.
A concept from Donald Winnicott: sensitive responsiveness most of the time is enough; perfection is not required.
Designed by Tronick: the mother suddenly goes blank-faced, and the infant's attempts to bring the interaction back are observed.

quotes.text: And it's the best defense that they could come up with.
Mary Main coined these three very powerful words, "fright without solution" so that you are in a very frightening place and you don't know how to get, you don't know what to do.

As a human species, we're really resilient. There's a lot that we can absorb in the not getting it quite right, and in fact, even the securely attached, it's less than 50% of the time that there's an attune moment.

And I think that's such a helpful concept for parents out there that the securely attached mother is the good enough mother who is there most of the time in a responsive, sensitive way, not a hundred percent of the time because it's not even possible.

So it's not so much what happened in your childhood, but what you make of those experiences and the flexibility in being able to think about different scenarios in your head, why people behaved as they did, and to do so in a coherent way.
So the two words that go with secure attachment are flexibility and coherence. Does your story have a beginning, middle, and end?
I think the stepping aside is often even for 30 seconds saying, you know what? Mommy's really upset right now. I'm just going to take a moment, is another way of alerting your child.
